Protracted

pro-TRAK-tid -- from Latin pro- ('forward') + trahere ('to drag'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Protracted is drawn out or lasting for far longer than expected.

The two companies finally settled after a protracted legal battle that dragged on for nearly seven years.

Worked Example

What should have been a quick outpatient procedure turned into a protracted hospital stay lasting almost a month.

Notice the mismatch between expectation and reality -- a quick procedure was supposed to be over fast, but it dragged on far longer than anyone planned. That gap between 'should have been short' and 'actually went on and on' is exactly what protracted captures.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lengthy: Lengthy just means taking a long time, with no complaint built in -- a lengthy report may be perfectly normal for its kind. Protracted adds the drag: something protracted has stretched far past what anyone expected or wanted, well beyond merely long.

long-winded: Long-winded describes a speaker or piece of writing that uses far more words than needed. Protracted measures time, not wordiness -- a protracted debate drags on the clock for hours or months, while a long-winded answer can wander and still be over in a minute.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

brief: lasting only a short time

swift: happening quickly, with little delay

Where it sits · how endlessly it drags on — prolonged → protracted → interminable

prolonged vs. protracted: Prolonged is milder than protracted: a prolonged wait is simply longer than usual, while a protracted one drags on so far past every estimate that people begin to lose hope of an end.

interminable vs. protracted: Interminable is stronger than protracted: a protracted meeting does eventually end, however slowly, but an interminable one feels as though no end will ever come at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forward (Latin)

root — -tract-

root — -tract-: to drag, to pull (Latin (trahere))

Put it together

Put it together: Protracted comes from Latin pro- ('forward') plus trahere ('to drag') -- literally 'dragged forward' -- so something protracted feels like it's being pulled out, stretched far beyond how long it should have reasonably taken.

Use the root in a new word: attract

Use the root in a new word: attract: The bright porch light seemed to attract every moth in the neighborhood.

Root Check

Word Choice

Protracted is about a process or event lasting much longer than expected -- a protracted negotiation, a protracted illness. Compare Linger, which is about a lingering presence, like a smell or a feeling, not a whole extended process.
